title: Total hip replacement (posterior approach)
subtitle: Primary hip arthroplasty through the posterior approach

indications: End-stage hip arthritis (osteoarthritis, inflammatory arthritis, avascular necrosis, post-traumatic or dysplastic arthritis) with pain and loss of function that persist despite non-operative treatment.
Selected displaced intracapsular hip fractures in patients who walked independently outdoors with no more than a stick, are not cognitively impaired and are medically fit (NICE CG124).
Decision based on symptoms and their effect on life, not on a radiographic or score threshold alone.
contraindications: Active infection in the hip or elsewhere (including skin ulcers and urinary infection) until treated.
Medical comorbidity that makes the risk of a major elective operation unacceptable after optimisation.
Neuropathic joint or a non-functioning abductor mechanism: relative, because of instability.
Poor skin over the incision site, or a patient unable to engage with rehabilitation: relative.
preparation: Anteroposterior pelvis and lateral hip radiographs with a calibration marker; template cup size, stem size, neck cut level, offset and leg length.
Preoperative assessment: anaemia, diabetes control, skin, dental and urinary sources of infection, MRSA screening per local policy, and an anaesthetic review.
Plan blood management: tranexamic acid unless contraindicated, and group and save.

Consent risks to discuss: infection, dislocation, leg length difference, nerve injury (sciatic and its common peroneal division), periprosthetic fracture, venous thromboembolism, bleeding, wound problems, persistent pain, loosening and later revision, and the risks of anaesthesia and death.
positioning: Lateral decubitus with the operated side up, secured with pelvic supports on the pubic symphysis and the sacrum so the pelvis is truly vertical and cannot roll.
Pad the down-side fibular head, axilla (axillary roll) and arm; check the down-side leg pulses.
Confirm the pelvis is perpendicular to the floor before draping: it is the reference for cup orientation.
equipment: Laminar flow theatre, hoods or body exhaust per local policy, and the templated implant system with the full range of sizes and a backup.
Acetabular reamers, femoral broaches, trial heads and necks, cement gun and restrictor if cemented, pulsatile lavage.
Cerclage wires or cables available for a calcar crack; high-speed drill for trochanteric holes.
anatomy: The sciatic nerve emerges below piriformis and runs over the short external rotators and quadratus femoris; the peroneal division is the more lateral and more vulnerable part.
The medial femoral circumflex artery runs deep to quadratus femoris and gives the ascending branches; it bleeds when quadratus is divided.
The transverse acetabular ligament defines the inferior margin of the acetabulum and helps judge native anteversion.
The acetabular quadrant system: posterosuperior is the safest for screws, the anterior quadrants overlie the external iliac and obturator vessels.
criticalSafety: Confirm the side and implant availability at the time-out, and check the pelvis is truly vertical before cup insertion.
Protect the sciatic nerve throughout: retractors, leg position during dislocation and reduction, and lengthening.
Cement safety pause with the anaesthetist before any cement goes in.
Repair the posterior capsule and rotators.
structuresAtRisk: Sciatic nerve, particularly its peroneal division
Superior and inferior gluteal neurovascular bundles
External iliac and obturator vessels (acetabular screws or medial perforation)
Femoral nerve and vessels (anterior retractor placed too far medially)
commonErrors: Cup inserted with the pelvis rolled forward, giving a retroverted or vertical cup.
Stem placed in varus or excessive retroversion.
Omitting the posterior soft-tissue repair at the end of a long case.
complications: Dislocation, early or late, often related to component position or soft-tissue failure.
Periprosthetic joint infection, superficial wound infection and wound ooze.
Leg length discrepancy and abductor dysfunction.
Sciatic or common peroneal nerve palsy.
Venous thromboembolism, bleeding requiring transfusion, bone cement implantation syndrome.
Heterotopic ossification, aseptic loosening and wear needing revision.
postop: Mobilise with physiotherapy on the day of surgery where possible, with weight bearing as the implant fixation allows.
Posterior hip precautions per local protocol, with clear written advice.
Extended thromboprophylaxis for the duration set by NICE NG89 for hip replacement, with mechanical prophylaxis while in hospital.
Haemoglobin check, wound review, neurovascular observations including foot dorsiflexion, and a postoperative radiograph.
Follow-up with outcome scores and registry submission per national practice.

steps.emphasis: Template on calibrated films. Mark the side, and confirm the implant system and sizes are available.
Antibiotic per local arthroplasty policy before incision; tranexamic acid unless contraindicated; extended VTE prophylaxis planned.
Lateral with rigid supports on the symphysis and sacrum. The pelvis must be vertical; a forward-rolled pelvis retroverts the cup.
Before dislocating, mark a leg length reference (for example a pin in the ilium and a mark on the trochanter) to compare with later.
Use the tibia held vertical as the guide to stem anteversion.
Posterior stability: flexion to 90 degrees, adduction and internal rotation. Anterior stability: extension with external rotation. Check for impingement and compare length with the reference.
For a cemented stem. For an uncemented stem, impact to a press fit and check for calcar cracks instead.
Ask the patient to dorsiflex the ankle and extend the toes in recovery once the block allows: the peroneal division is the one at risk.

step.thr.acetabulum-prep.title: Acetabular exposure and reaming
step.thr.acetabulum-prep.why: The cup can only be placed well in an acetabulum that is fully seen. Reaming creates a hemispherical bed of bleeding bone for fixation while keeping enough of the walls and subchondral plate to support the cup.
how: Place retractors anteriorly over the anterior wall, posteriorly behind the posterior wall over the reflected rotators, and inferiorly at the transverse acetabular ligament; keep the posterior retractor off the sciatic nerve.
Excise the labrum and pulvinar, remove osteophytes, and identify the transverse acetabular ligament and the floor of the cotyloid fossa.
Ream to the medial floor first with a small reamer, then enlarge in steps in the planned orientation until bleeding subchondral bone is reached around the rim.
Check the walls after each size: stop if the anterior or posterior wall is being thinned.
structuresAtRisk: Obturator vessels near the transverse ligament
pitfalls: Reaming in a vertical or retroverted direction because the pelvis has rolled forward on the table.
Retractor levered hard on the posterior column against the sciatic nerve.

step.thr.cup.title: Acetabular component orientation and fixation
step.thr.cup.why: Cup inclination and anteversion are the main surgeon-controlled factors in dislocation, wear and impingement. The pelvis is rarely exactly where you think it is in the lateral position, so use more than one reference.
how: Recheck pelvic position on the table before inserting the cup.

Aim for the planned inclination and anteversion, commonly within the Lewinnek safe zone, using the transverse acetabular ligament and the bony rim as references, not only the external alignment guide.

For an uncemented cup, impact it to a press fit and confirm seating through the apical hole. If screws are needed, place them in the posterosuperior quadrant; the anterior quadrants risk the external iliac and obturator vessels.
For a cemented cup, prepare keying holes, lavage and dry the bone, pressurise the cement, and hold the cup still in the planned orientation until set.
Trim overhanging osteophytes that could cause impingement, and insert the liner after checking that the rim is clean.
structuresAtRisk: External iliac vessels and obturator vessels (anterior screws)
Superior gluteal neurovascular bundle (long posterosuperior screws)
pitfalls: Relying on the mechanical guide alone when the pelvis has tilted.
Screws placed in the anterior quadrants.
Incompletely seated cup with a gap at the dome.
